reference_title: Design and Construction of Driven Pile Foundations

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Without a thorough foundation study the result is (1) a foundation with a large safety margin, usually more expensive and sometimes hard to build, (2) an unsafe foundation, or (3) construction disputes and claims. Site characterization is the subsurface exploration and testing that give the geomaterial parameters; for reliability based design, reducing uncertainty in properties may give more economical foundations. Guidance: FHWA-NHI-01-031, GEC-5, FHWA-NHI-06-088; testing in Chapter 5.
sections.body: (pp. 79-80) Foundation design needs adequate knowledge of the subsurface. Without a thorough foundation study or adequate geotechnical data the result is often (1) a foundation with a large safety margin, generally more expensive and sometimes difficult to construct, (2) an unsafe foundation, or (3) construction disputes and claims. Site characterization is a subsurface exploration program and the testing that gives geomaterial parameters for design, also used in construction feasibility and planning; for reliability based design, reducing uncertainty in geomaterial properties may lead to more economical foundations. The chapter assumes a driven pile foundation has been selected. An experienced geotechnical engineer helps plan the exploration, order field and laboratory tests, set the design subsurface profile and recommend feasible foundations, and compiles specialty firms' results into a geotechnical design report used by several disciplines (some agencies use design memoranda and transmittals instead, which needs regular communication). Guidance: FHWA-NHI-01-031 (Mayne et al. 2002), GEC-5 (Sabatini et al. 2002) and FHWA-NHI-06-088 (Samtani and Nowatzki 2006); laboratory and in-situ testing are in Chapter 5.
key_points: Inadequate geotechnical data leads to an over-conservative and costly foundation, an unsafe foundation, or disputes and claims
Site characterization: subsurface exploration plus testing to determine geomaterial design parameters
Reducing uncertainty in geomaterial properties may lead to more economical foundations in reliability based design
The geotechnical engineer plans exploration and testing, sets the design profile and compiles the geotechnical design report
Guidance: FHWA-NHI-01-031 (Mayne et al. 2002), GEC-5 (Sabatini et al. 2002), FHWA-NHI-06-088
Laboratory and in-situ testing are discussed in Chapter 5
sections.applicability: Overview of the site characterization program for driven pile foundation projects.

sections.title: Site Characterization Program
sections.summary: Three exploration phases: (1) office data collection, (2) field reconnaissance, and (3) detailed subsurface exploration (borings, sampling, in-situ testing). Each phase builds on the previous. Single-phase programs common for small projects; staged programs for large or design-build projects.
sections.body: (p. 80) Site characterization encompasses gathering and reporting site conditions required to safely and economically design foundations. The information needed varies depending on site geologic conditions, foundation types, structural performance requirements, acceptable risk, and constructability. The site exploration consists of three main phases: (1) planning the exploration program and data collection (office work), (2) field reconnaissance survey, and (3) detailed subsurface exploration (boring, sampling, and in-situ testing). Table 4-1 lists the purpose of each phase.
key_points: Three exploration phases: office planning, field reconnaissance, detailed subsurface exploration
Each phase adds to or supplements the previous phase
Single-phase programs common for small projects; staged programs for large or design-build projects
Information must address geologic conditions, foundation types, performance requirements, and constructability
tables: Table 4-1: Subsurface Exploration Phases (p. 81) - columns: Phase; Activity; Purpose; Remarks (each cell below is named by its column). 1. Activity: Planning the Exploration (Office Work). Purpose: A. Obtain structure information and determine: 1. Type of structure. 2. Preliminary location of piers and abutments. 3. Loading and special design events. 4. Allowable differential settlement, lateral deformations, and other performance criteria. 5. Any special features and requirements. B. Obtain drilling records for nearby structures and from local well drillers. C. Perform literature reviews including maintenance records, pile driving records, scour history, etc. Obtain overall picture of subsurface conditions in the area. Remarks: See Table 4-2 for sources of information. | 2. Activity: Field Reconnaissance Survey. Purpose: Verify information gained from the office phase and plan the detailed subsurface exploration. A. Observe, confirm and collect information regarding: 1. Topographic, geologic, and hydrologic features. 2. New and old construction in the area including utilities. Performance of existing structures. 3. Drilling equipment required, cost, and access for the equipment. B. If appropriate, conduct geophysical testing to obtain preliminary subsurface information. Remarks: Field reconnaissance is often conducted by a multi-disciplined team. | 3. Activity: Detailed Subsurface Exploration. Purpose: Develop a preliminary boring plan based on phases 1 and 2. Conduct a preliminary evaluation for viable foundation systems including ground improvement. Determine subsurface requirements for all of the viable foundation systems. The boring plan should be modified if needed as the borings are performed and detailed subsurface information is obtained. The subsurface exploration should provide the following: 1. Depth and thickness of strata (subsurface profile). 2. In-situ field tests to determine soil design parameters. 3. Samples to determine soil and rock design parameters. 4. Groundwater levels including perched, regional, and any artesian conditions. Remarks: For major structures, the pilot boring program is often supplemented with control and verification boring programs.
sections.applicability: Framework for organizing and executing a subsurface exploration program for driven pile projects.

sections.title: Data Collection
sections.summary: Office phase: gather structural information from bridge design office plus general subsurface data from geotechnical databases, topographic maps (USGS), agricultural soil surveys (USDA), aerial photos, well records, and geologic maps (Table 4-2). Prepares engineer for field reconnaissance and identifies problem areas.
sections.body: (pp. 80-83) The data collection phase obtains information about the proposed structure and general subsurface conditions. Structural information comes from the bridge design office and preliminary structure plans. General subsurface information is obtained from a variety of sources listed in Table 4-2, including geotechnical databases, construction records, topographic maps (USGS), county agricultural soil survey maps (USDA), aerial photos or satellite imagery, well drilling records, and geologic maps. This phase prepares the engineer for the field reconnaissance survey and identifies possible problems and areas to scrutinize. Approach embankment preliminary design and performance requirements come from the roadway office.
key_points: Obtain structural information from bridge design office and preliminary structure plans
Sources of subsurface information include geotechnical databases, construction records, topographic maps, aerial photos, well drilling records, and geologic maps
Data collection prepares the engineer for field reconnaissance
Identifies possible problems and areas requiring additional scrutiny
Additional sources of historical data are listed in GEC-5, Sabatini et al. (2002)
tables: Table 4-2: Sources of Subsurface Information and Use (p. 82) - columns: Source; Use (each row below as 'Source: ... Use: ...'). Source: Preliminary structure plans prepared by the bridge design office. Use: Determine: 1. Type of structure. 2. Preliminary locations of piers and abutments. 3. Footing loads and special design events. 4. Allowable differential settlement, lateral deformations, and performance criteria. 5. Any special features and requirements. | Source: Geotechnical databases. Use: Nearby soil boring logs, laboratory test results, and in-situ test results. | Source: Construction plans and records for nearby structures. Use: Foundation type, old boring data, construction information including construction problems. | Source: Topographic maps prepared by the United States Coast and Geodetic Survey (USC and GS), United States Geological Survey (USGS) and State Geology survey. Use: Existing physical features shown; find landform boundaries and determine access for exploration equipment. Maps from different dates can be used to determine topographic changes over time. | Source: County agricultural soil survey maps and reports prepared by the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA). Use: Boundaries of landforms shown; appraisal of general shallow subsurface conditions. | Source: Aerial photos prepared by the United States Geological Survey (USGS) or satellite imagery such as Google Earth. Use: Detailed physical relief shown; gives indication of major problems such as old landslide scars, fault scarps, buried meander channels, sinkholes, or scour; provides basis for field reconnaissance. | Source: Well drilling record or water supply bulletins from state geology or water resources department. Use: Old well records or borings with general soils data shown; estimate required depth of explorations and preliminary cost of foundations. | Source: Geologic maps and Geology bulletins. Use: Type, depth and orientation of rock formations.
sections.applicability: Office-based data collection phase of site characterization for driven pile foundation design.

sections.title: Field Reconnaissance Survey
sections.summary: Site visit to identify constructability issues (access, headroom, utilities), inspect nearby structures for foundation performance, check stream banks for scour, and examine terrain for landslides. Findings guide boring program planning. Example reconnaissance form per AASHTO Foundation Investigation Manual (1978).
sections.body: (pp. 83-85) Site visits by the geotechnical engineer and other design team members are necessary to properly characterize the site. Field reconnaissance presents an opportunity to locate and record constructability issues such as site access, headroom restrictions, and other working conditions that may be overlooked from reviewing site or aerial photos. The field reconnaissance includes inspection of nearby structures, inspection of existing footings and stream banks for scour, recording of existing structures, visual examination for evidence of landslides, location of trees and surface water, and relating site conditions to proposed boring operations. Figure 4-1 contains an example of a field reconnaissance form modified from the AASHTO Foundation Investigation Manual (1978).
key_points: Site visits are necessary to verify and supplement office phase information
Locate and record constructability issues: site access, headroom, utilities
Inspect nearby structures for foundation performance
Check existing footings and stream banks for evidence of scour and movement
Examine terrain for evidence of landslides
Record features and constraints that impact constructability of potential foundation systems
Geotechnical loading requirements dictate field exploration program planning
sections.applicability: Field reconnaissance phase of site characterization for driven pile foundations.

sections.title: Detailed Field Exploration
sections.summary: Detailed borings, sampling, and in-situ testing form the factual basis for pile design. Major structures use a two-phase approach: pilot borings during planning for preliminary profile, then control borings at key locations and verification borings to fill gaps. Geophysical surveys and in-situ testing supplement conventional borings.
sections.body: (p. 85) The purpose of the field exploration program is to obtain representative information on subsurface conditions, to recover disturbed and undisturbed soil samples, to perform in-situ testing, and to determine groundwater levels. This information provides the factual basis for all subsequent steps in pile design and construction. The field exploration plan focuses on items related to the design of driven pile foundations. For major structures, pilot borings are performed at select locations during preliminary planning to establish a preliminary subsurface profile, followed by a two-phase boring program: control borings at key locations, then verification borings to fill in gaps.
key_points: Provides factual basis for all subsequent pile design and construction steps
Quality and completeness of subsurface data are paramount
First step is a preliminary boring, sampling, and in-situ testing plan
For major structures: pilot borings during planning, then control + verification borings
Geophysical surveys and in-situ testing supplement conventional borings
Preliminary structural design plan should be established to ensure borings are properly located
sections.applicability: Detailed subsurface exploration planning for driven pile foundation design.

sections.title: Geophysical Surveys
sections.summary: Geophysical surveys supplement borings over large areas. Seismic and electrical methods give depth to groundwater, bedrock and strata; seismic surface wave methods assess soil stiffness; ground penetrating radar finds near-surface voids in the 20 to 30 ft range but is not useful in saturated clays; electrical resistivity distinguishes coarse from fine-grained materials and locates groundwater. Always combine with direct exploration (borings, in-situ tests).
sections.body: (pp. 85-86) Geophysical surveys aid in subsurface characterization over a wide area and supplement borings and other invasive tests. Primarily, seismic and electrical methods are used to measure depth to groundwater and bedrock and to resolve intermediate soil strata thickness. These methods may identify and locate subsurface anomalies requiring further evaluation by soil borings or in-situ tests. Geophysical surveys may also locate voids, debris, or buried objects as well as measure divisions in soil stiffness. Seismic surface wave methods use impact or ambient noise to produce surface waves analyzed for soil stiffness, bedrock depth, and groundwater depth. Ground penetrating radar detects near-surface voids in the 20-30 foot depth range but is not effective in saturated clayey soils. Electrical resistivity measures soil strata changes and locates voids or buried objects.
key_points: Supplement borings and other invasive tests over a wide area
Seismic and electrical methods measure depth to groundwater, bedrock, and soil strata thickness
Can locate voids, debris, buried objects, and subsurface anomalies
Seismic surface wave methods analyze soil stiffness from reflected waves
Ground penetrating radar useful for near-surface voids (20-30 ft) but not in saturated clays
Electrical resistivity can distinguish coarse vs fine-grained materials and locate groundwater
Should always be performed in combination with direct exploration methods (borings, in-situ tests)
sections.applicability: Non-invasive subsurface characterization to supplement boring and in-situ testing programs.

sections.title: Depth, Spacing, and Frequency of Boring and In-Situ Tests
sections.summary: Minimum exploration points (Table 4-3): one per substructure for width W <= 100 ft, two for W > 100 ft. Borings extend at least 20 ft below the expected pile toe, or at least two times the pile group width; for piles on rock, at least 10 ft of rock coring. Borings must pass through unsuitable strata (peat, organics, uncontrolled fill, soft fine-grained and loose coarse-grained soils) to suitable support. Erratic conditions need closer spacing; site geology may require more.
sections.body: (pp. 86-87) The cost of a subsurface exploration program is small relative to the foundation cost; however, in the absence of adequate boring data, the engineer must rely on conservative designs with high safety margins. The number of borings, their spacing, and sampling intervals depend on the uniformity of soil strata and loading conditions. Table 4-3 provides minimum quantity guidelines for exploration points per substructure. Minimum exploration depths should extend 20 feet below expected pile toe elevation, or at least two times the pile group width. For piles on rock, at least 10 feet of rock coring should be performed. In-situ test spacing and frequency should be determined based on project requirements, supplementing borings where undisturbed sampling is not easily performed. For example, one 2.4 inch diameter boring costs less than one 12 inch diameter pile. Where peat, highly organic materials, uncontrolled fills, soft fine grained soils or loose coarse-grained soils are met, borings should extend through them to suitable support.
key_points: Exploration cost is small against foundation cost: one 2.4 in. boring costs less than one 12 in. pile
Erratic subsurface conditions require closely spaced borings
W <= 100 ft: minimum 1 exploration point per substructure; W > 100 ft: minimum 2 points
Minimum depth: 20 ft below expected pile toe or 2x pile group width
For piles on rock: at least 10 ft of rock coring
Additional boring and in-situ testing depths may be required due to site-specific geology
Borings should extend through unsuitable soil strata (peat, highly organic material, uncontrolled fill, soft fine-grained, loose coarse-grained soils) to reach suitable foundation support materials
Liquefaction and aggressive environment studies may dictate appropriate sampling intervals

W ≤ 100-ft; 1 | W > 100-ft; 2. Footnote: ^1 Additional exploration points should be provided if erratic subsurface conditions are encountered.
sections.applicability: Guidelines for boring layout and depth for driven pile site characterization programs.

sections.title: Soil Boring Methods
sections.summary: Soil borings are the most frequently used exploration technique (Table 4-4): auger borings (most equipment to 100-200 ft; a hollow stem auger acts as a casing), rotary drilling (200 ft or more; suited to 4-6 in. holes; most rapid in most soils and rock), wash borings (100 ft or more; light, inexpensive equipment, slow, not suited to stones and boulders; infrequently used in the U.S.), and sonic coring (up to 1000 ft, generally 100% recovery in soil and bedrock). Drilling mud can contaminate recovered samples.
sections.body: (pp. 88-89) Soil borings are the most frequently used exploration technique and offer the ability to collect disturbed and undisturbed samples and to perform in-situ tests. Common methods include augered borings, wash borings, rotary drilling, and sonic drilling, summarized in Table 4-4. Continuous flight augers (solid or hollow stem) bore into the subsurface for sampling and testing; hollow stem augers act as casing and range from 2.25 to 12.25 inch I.D. Rotary drilling uses a drill bit to cut and grind material, with water or drilling mud flushing cuttings. Wash borings are advanced by chopping action of a light bit with water jetting. Sonic coring can collect any soil type with minimal fluids up to 1000 feet. A solid stem auger must be removed to test native soil, so it is not useful in soft soils, sands or high groundwater and suits shallow sampling only.
key_points: Auger borings: most common, can drill to 100-200 ft; hollow stem acts as casing
Solid stem augers must be withdrawn to test; not useful in soft soils, sands or high groundwater
Rotary drilling: suited for 4-6 inch diameter borings to 200+ ft; rapid method in most soils and rock
Wash borings: light equipment, inexpensive, but slow and not suited for stones/boulders
Sonic coring: up to 1000 ft, generally 100% recovery, collects soils and bedrock with minimal fluids
Drilling mud can contaminate recovered soil samples
Wash borings infrequently used in the United States
tables: Table 4-4: Soil Boring Methods (p. 89) - columns: Method; Depth; Advantages; Disadvantages; Remarks (each cell below is named by its column). Auger Borings. Depth: Most equipment can drill to depths of 100 to 200 feet. Advantages: Boring advanced without water or drilling mud. Hollow stem auger acts as a casing. Disadvantages: Difficult to detect change in material. Heavy equipment required. Water level must be maintained in boring equal to or greater than existing water table to prevent sample disturbance. Remarks: Boring advanced by rotating and simultaneously pressing an auger into the ground either mechanically or hydraulically. | Rotary Drilling. Depth: Most equipment can drill to depths of 200 feet or more. Advantages: Suited for borings 4 to 6 inches in diameter. Most rapid method in most soils and rock. Relatively uniform hole with little disturbance to the soil below the bottom of hole. Experienced driller can detect changes based on rate of progress. Disadvantages: Drilling mud if used does not provide an indication of material change as the wash water does. Use of drilling mud hampers the performance of permeability tests. Remarks: Borehole advanced by rapid rotation of drilling bit and removal of material by water or drilling mud. Rock coring is performed by rotary drilling. Liquefaction evaluation methods require mud rotary drilling methods. | Wash Boring. Depth: Most equipment can drill to depths of 100 feet or more. Advantages: Borings of small and large diameter. Equipment is relatively inexpensive. Equipment is light. Wash water provides an indication of change in materials. Disadvantages: Slow rate of progress. Not suitable for materials containing stones and boulders. Remarks: Boring advanced by a combination of the chopping action of a light bit and jetting action of the water coming through the bit. | Sonic Coring. Depth: Up to 1000 feet. Advantages: Generally a 100% recovery rate. Can collect samples in soils and bedrock. Disadvantages: Expensive for large amounts of dense rock sampling. Remarks: Borehole advanced in 10 feet cased sections. Can collect any soil type with minimal to no fluids.
sections.applicability: Selection of soil boring methods for driven pile site characterization programs.

sections.title: Soil Sampling Methods
sections.summary: Disturbed samples: split barrel (SPT) sampler (1.375 in. ID, 2 in. OD, ASTM D1586), sonic cores, or test pits. Undisturbed samples: thin-walled (Shelby) tubes (ASTM D1587) for fine-grained soils, piston samplers (keep soil out of the tube before sampling), or the Pitcher sampler (alternating hard and soft layers). No sample is completely undisturbed.
sections.body: (pp. 88-91) Soil samples may be collected via disturbed or undisturbed methods. Disturbed samples are collected with a split barrel sampler, sonic cores, or test pits and are used for visual classification and routine laboratory testing. The standard split spoon sampler for SPT has an inner diameter of 1.375 inches and outer diameter of 2 inches (ASTM D1586), shown in Figure 4-2. Relatively undisturbed samples are collected with thin walled tubes (Shelby tubes, Figure 4-3), piston samplers, or the Pitcher sampler. Thin walled tubes are typically used for fine-grained soils; piston samplers prevent soil from entering the tube prematurely; the Pitcher sampler can sample alternating hard and soft layers. ASTM D1587 provides detailed guidance on thin walled tube sampling. Split barrel samplers typically range from 1.5 to 2.5 inches in diameter and are 18 or 24 inches long; disturbed samples are not suitable for strength or compressibility testing.
key_points: Disturbed samples: split barrel sampler (SPT), sonic cores, or test pits
Standard SPT sampler: 1.375 in ID, 2 in OD (ASTM D1586)
Split barrel samplers: 1.5 to 2.5 in. diameter, 18 or 24 in. long; disturbed samples not for strength or compressibility tests
Undisturbed samples: thin walled tubes (Shelby tubes, ASTM D1587), piston samplers, Pitcher sampler
No sample will be completely undisturbed even with utmost care
Thin walled tubes are typically used for fine-grained soils
Piston samplers prevent soil from entering tube before sampling
Pitcher sampler is attractive for alternating hard and soft layers
figures: Figure 4-3: Shelby tubes (after Mayne et al. 2002) (p. 91)
sections.applicability: Soil sampling equipment and techniques for driven pile site characterization programs.

sections.title: Rock Exploration Methods (Coring / Drilling)
sections.summary: Rock coring follows the soil boring at bedrock: conventional rotary, wire line rotary (preferred below 80 ft for faster retrieval), and methods for swelling clay and soft rock. RQD (ASTM D6032) = sum of sound core pieces >= 4 in. / total run length: Excellent 90-100%, Good 75-90%, Fair 50-75%, Poor 25-50%, Very Poor < 25%. Cores are boxed with notes on bedding, fractures and weathering and kept beyond the project for claims. RQD alone should not be used to correlate rock strength.
sections.body: (pp. 91-94) Rock drilling and coring is typically performed at the end of a soil boring once bedrock is encountered. Special drilling bits cut and grind through rock while fluid or air flushes out cuttings. The recovered rock core is classified by rock type, recovery length, and recovery percentage. Table 4-5 summarizes rock coring methods: conventional rotary coring, wire line rotary coring (preferred for depths > 80 ft), and rotary coring of swelling clay or soft rock. Rock cores should be stored in structurally sound core boxes (Figure 4-4) with careful notation of bedding, fractures, and weathered zones. Rock cores are given a Rock Quality Designation (RQD) per ASTM D6032, defined as the sum of sound core pieces >= 4 inches in length divided by the total core run length, expressed as a percentage. Table 4-6 provides RQD designations: Excellent (90-100), Good (75-90), Fair (50-75), Poor (25-50), Very Poor (<25). Deere and Deere (1989; printed 'Deere and Deer') proposed the RQD; core lengths are measured along the axis centerline. A swelling clay or soft rock barrel has a third inner liner, removed more easily owing to the 5 to 10 % difference in liner and bit size (Acker 1974).
key_points: Rock coring performed after soil boring encounters bedrock
Conventional rotary, wire line rotary, and swelling clay/soft rock coring methods available
Wire line rotary coring preferred for depths > 80 ft due to faster retrieval
Rock cores stored in core boxes with notation of bedding, fractures, and weathering
RQD (ASTM D6032) = sum of sound core pieces >= 4 in / total core run length
RQD designations: Excellent (90-100), Good (75-90), Fair (50-75), Poor (25-50), Very Poor (<25)
Core samples should be retained for project duration and beyond for construction claims
RQD alone should not be used to correlate rock strength

Conventional Rotary Coring in Rock. Depth: Most equipment can drill to depths of 200 feet or more. Type of Samples Taken: Continuous Rock Cores. Advantages: Helps differentiate between boulders and bedrock. Disadvantages: Can be slow and fairly expensive. Remarks: Several types of core barrels are used. | Wire Line Rotary Coring in Rock. sections.applicability: Rock exploration and quality assessment for driven pile foundations bearing on or driven to rock.

sections.title: Groundwater
sections.summary: Monitor water levels during drilling, at boring completion, and 24 hours after; low-permeability cohesive soils may require > 1 week for equilibrium. Observation wells (slotted PVC) monitor unconfined water table; piezometers (pneumatic or vibrating wire) monitor confined aquifer hydrostatic pressure. Essential for effective stress analysis and construction dewatering planning.
sections.body: (pp. 94-95) Accurate groundwater level information is needed for estimating soil densities, determining effective soil pressures, preparing effective stress diagrams, and indicating construction difficulties that may be encountered. Water levels should be monitored during drilling, upon completion of boring, and 24 hours after completion. More than one week may be required for representative readings in low-permeability cohesive soils or bore holes stabilized with drilling muds. Observation wells (slotted PVC pipe) monitor water level changes in a select aquifer, while piezometers (pneumatic or vibrating wire diaphragm devices) monitor hydrostatic pressure changes in a confined aquifer or specific stratum. Additional piezometer information is available in FHWA-NHI-01-031 (Mayne et al. 2002).
key_points: Groundwater levels needed for soil density estimation, effective stress calculations, and construction planning
Monitor water levels during drilling, at boring completion, and 24 hours after
Low permeability soils may require > 1 week for representative water level readings
Observation wells (slotted PVC pipe) for unconfined water table monitoring
Piezometers (pneumatic or vibrating wire) for confined aquifer hydrostatic pressure monitoring
Single and multiple piezometers can be installed in a single bore hole
sections.applicability: Groundwater characterization for effective stress analysis and construction planning in driven pile projects.

sections.title: Information Required for Construction
sections.summary: Site characterization data drives: pile type selection, hammer sizing, installation aid determination (predrilling, jetting), cost estimation, bid documents, construction control methods, and schedules. Pile type from local practice, structural requirements, and subsurface conditions; size and length from soil properties and bearing layers. Well-defined characterization reduces unplanned cost and contractor claims.
sections.body: (p. 95) The subsurface exploration and subsequent soil and rock testing program provides essential information for driven pile design and construction. Engineers and contractors use this information to select pile type, size hammer equipment, determine if installation aids are needed, prepare cost estimates and bid documents, establish construction control methods, and generate construction schedules. Pile type is generally selected based on local practice, structural requirements, and subsurface conditions, while size and length depend on soil properties and bearing layers. Pile drivability and other construction considerations are affected by the overall site characterization including permeability, relative density, layering, and soil response to pile driving.
key_points: Subsurface data essential for pile type selection, hammer sizing, and installation aid determination
Used to prepare cost estimates, bid documents, and construction schedules
Pile type selected based on local practice, structural requirements, and subsurface conditions
Pile size and length depend on soil properties and bearing layers
Drivability affected by permeability, relative density, layering, and soil response to driving
Well-defined site characterization reduces risk of unplanned cost and claims
sections.applicability: Use of site characterization data for driven pile construction planning and cost estimation.
